definition: Ostracism means exclusion from a group by deliberate shunning.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word ostracism. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know ostracism should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: New hires who skipped the union picnic learned that a season of quiet ostracism could be colder than any reprimand.
A snub is a single icy moment — one greeting refused, one invitation withheld; ostracism is that treatment organized and sustained by the whole group.
Banishment goes further than ostracism: the group does not merely freeze you out of its company, it formally casts you out of the place itself.

Exclusion is the broadest term for being left out — by rule, by chance, or by design, once or always. Ostracism is one specific kind: deliberate, sustained shunning by a group of one of its own, enforced through cold behavior rather than any written rule.

Shunning is the pointed avoidance itself — the turned backs, the unreturned greetings — and a single person can shun another. Ostracism is that treatment organized and sustained: a whole group closing ranks against one member and keeping the freeze going for weeks.

Naturalists describe ostracism among ravens: a bird that steals from the shared cache is driven to the edge of the roost, and for weeks none of the others will feed beside it.
Ostracism is more specific than rejection because it is exclusion enforced by the group's own behavior — no ruling, no announcement, just a closing of ranks that leaves one member outside them.
Ostracism is the analyst's word for group-enforced exclusion — sociable animals, playgrounds, and office floors all practice it.
It needs no official act; the freeze itself is the punishment.

Psychologist Kipling Williams began studying ostracism after a frisbee landed at his feet in a park: two strangers tossed it with him for a minute, then, without a word, stopped throwing it his way.
The strangers owed him nothing, yet the freeze-out stung — and the sting became his career.
In his lab, volunteers play a three-way computer game of catch.
Partway through, the other two players — actually the program — simply stop passing the ball to them.
Even knowing it is only software, players report a sharp drop in mood; being pointedly left out by the group, again and again, registers almost like physical pain.
The lesson, Williams argues, is that ostracism needs no insult and no exile: a group's quiet, repeated refusal to include one person is punishment enough.
